chapters.title: Chapter 5 · The Elephant’s Child
chapters.artPrompt: a baby elephant kneeling at the edge of a grey-green river while a crocodile holds his little nose and pulls, tall reeds and melon patches around, bright African sunlight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: In the high and far-off times, the elephant had no trunk. He had only a blackish, bulgy nose, as big as a boot, that wiggled from side to side. And there was one elephant’s child who was full of questions. He asked the ostrich why her tail feathers grew just so, and the hippopotamus why her eyes were red. And every question got him a spanking.
The elephant’s child kneels by the great grey-green Limpopo River and meets the crocodile.

One morning he asked a new question. “What does the crocodile have for dinner?” he said. Then every uncle and aunt spanked him at once. But a kolokolo bird told him where to go. “Go to the banks of the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, and find out for yourself.” So the elephant’s child set off, eating melons all the way. Melons are sweet, and the road was long.
New word: curiosity — the wish to know about everything, which is how we learn.

At the river the crocodile winked one eye. “Come hither, little one,” he said, “and hear what I have for dinner.” The elephant’s child put his little nose down close — and the crocodile caught it and pulled! “I think today I begin with an elephant’s child!” he said. The little nose stretched and stretched, but it would not come off.

The bi-coloured python rock-snake came and helped to pull. At last the nose came free — but it was long and new. It was a trunk! Soon the child found it very useful. He could swat flies with it, pick grass with it, and dig for water. He could even wash the dust off his back.

When his uncles and aunts tried to spank him again, he swatted them all with his new trunk. Then every elephant went down to the Limpopo, one after another, to see the crocodile. And they all got trunks of their own. And that, from that day to this, is how the elephant got his trunk.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo
chapters.artPrompt: a kangaroo with long new legs flying over the golden Australian bush while a yellow dingo chases behind him under a great striped afternoon sun, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago, at noontime, a kangaroo came down to the wide blue Australian bush. In those days he had short fluffy legs and a little fluffy tail. He hopped about in tiny, dusty hops. He looked like a rabbit grown big — a rather plain animal — and nobody noticed him at all. The grass was grey with dust, and the sun was high.
The Yellow-Dog Dingo chases the kangaroo across the wide golden bush.

The kangaroo went to Little God Nqong, who was playing with the Yellow-Dog Dingo, and asked for a favour. The afternoon was warm, and the Dingo was sleepy in the sun. “I want to be different from all other animals by five o’clock this afternoon,” he said. Nqong turned to the Dingo. “Dingo!” he called. “That kangaroo says you are lazy. Catch him if you can!”
New word: favour — something kind that you ask another to do for you.

The Dingo bounded up with a growl, and the kangaroo fled. He hopped over the plains, round the gum-trees, across the grey desert and the golden sand. The Dingo followed over stone and sand, and never once gave up. And with every hop, his legs grew longer, and his tail grew thicker. And he went farther and farther with each jump.

By three o’clock his back legs were like stilts. By four he flew over the ground in great flying leaps. At five o’clock he could hardly hop another hop. He lay down on a rock, right in the middle of Australia, all hot and tired. The Dingo lay panting close behind.

“You’re different,” said Nqong. “You look like a kangaroo now.” And so he did. From that day to this, the kangaroo has had long hind legs and a thick tail. He flies over the ground in great hops — and the Dingo still chases him, sometimes. That is the sing-song of Old Man Kangaroo.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Beginning of the Armadillos
chapters.artPrompt: a small armadillo with a painted shell curling into a ball by a jungle river while a puzzled jaguar sits and watches, soft green forest light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: In the middle of South America there lived a Painted Jaguar. It was a warm green country, full of rivers and trees. His mother had taught him all she knew. “Stickly-Prickly Hedgehog curls up in a ball,” she said, “and Slow-and-Solid Tortoise swims away in the water. Curlers curl, and swimmers swim. Then you will always know which is which.”
The Painted Jaguar blinks at a curled-up hedgehog beside a tortoise swimming away.

One afternoon the Painted Jaguar found a hedgehog and a tortoise together by the river. The water was cool, and the sand was soft. The hedgehog rolled himself up into a little ball at once. The tortoise tucked in his legs, slid into the water, and swam. The jaguar looked from one to the other, quite confused. Should he curl? Should he swim? He did nothing at all.
New word: practise — to do a thing again and again, so that you learn to do it well.

That night the two friends talked it over. “He will come again tomorrow,” said the hedgehog. “Then let us teach each other our best tricks.” So the tortoise learned to tuck himself into a prickly ball, and the hedgehog learned to paddle and swim. All week the water splashed, and the shells shone. They practised day after day by the river.

Next week the Painted Jaguar came back, hungry. He found two little animals by the water. But one curled up — and it swam too! The other swam — and it curled as well! The jaguar sat down in the grass, more mixed up than ever, and went home without any supper at all.

And the two friends had grown snug little painted shells. From those two came all the armadillos in South America. They can curl up like a ball and swim like a fish. And to this day the jaguar has never been quite sure which is which. And that is the beginning of the armadillos.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · How the First Letter Was Written
chapters.artPrompt: a cave-man’s small daughter drawing a picture of fish and spears on a piece of tree bark with a shark’s tooth by a riverbank, soft morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Once, in the hills by the river Wagai, a cave-man named Tegumai went fishing with his little daughter Taffy. He caught a beautiful silver carp, but his spear broke in the fight, and the point stayed in the fish. The river was low that day, and the fish were plentiful. Taffy sat on a big stone, watching the water. While he sat mending it, a strange man came out of the bushes.
Taffy draws a picture on a piece of bark with her little shark’s tooth.

Taffy was a bright little girl, and she had a plan. She scratched a picture on a piece of bark. It showed her father with a broken spear, and herself, and her mother at the cave. Then she drew the stranger carrying the spare spear. “Take this to my mother,” she said, “and she will send the other spear.”
New word: bark — the rough outside skin of a tree.

But Taffy’s picture was not quite clear. The stranger ran to the cave with the bark, and Taffy’s mother thought the stranger had hurt Tegumai! The whole tribe came running with spears and stones. The river Wagai shook with shouting, and the fish fled. The poor stranger was chased and ducked in the river, till he was wetter than the fish.

Just then Tegumai and Taffy came home, dragging the carp, and everybody began to laugh. Taffy showed her picture and explained it all. The tribe was sorry for the stranger and made him welcome instead. Taffy’s mother dried the stranger’s coat, and they all sat down together. Tegumai hung the picture up in the cave to keep.

“If pictures could speak plainly,” said Tegumai, “we might send messages anywhere in the world.” So a picture could be a letter, if it were drawn well. And that was how the first letter was written — though the poor stranger got very wet over it.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · How the Alphabet Was Made
chapters.artPrompt: a cave-man and his small daughter scratching wiggly letter shapes on flat pieces of bark beside a warm cave fire, cosy evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: A week after the picture on the bark, Taffy and her father sat by the fire, making letters. The fire snapped, and the night was still outside the cave. It was the best fun they had ever had. They began with the carp, for Taffy had drawn it best of all. Tegumai scratched the fish shape on a flat piece of bark with a shark’s tooth. “This shape shall say ‘Ah!’” he said — and that was the letter A.
Taffy and Tegumai scratch the little letter shapes on flat pieces of bark.

Then they worked out more. A snake hisses ‘Sss’, so a wiggly snake shape was made for S. An egg standing up said ‘Eh’, and a round mouth said ‘Oh’. Little marks and dashes came too, for the small sounds between. The bark grew full of strange little signs. Every sound they needed got its own little picture, easy to scratch on bark or stone.
New word: alphabet — the set of letters we use for reading and writing.

Taffy thought of the shapes, and Tegumai made them plain. They laughed over the funny ones and argued over the crooked ones, and Taffy’s mother came and helped too. The cave smelled of smoke and warm bark. They worked by firelight till all the sounds had shapes. Bit by bit the whole set was finished, from A to the very last letter they could think of.

After that, Taffy and Tegumai could write anything at all, just by putting the little shapes together. They practised on bark and on stone, and the tribe learned them too. So the little pictures grew into letters, and the letters grew into words. And people have written ever since, all over the wide world. And that is how the alphabet was made — by a cave-man, his small daughter, and one little carp.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Crab That Played with the Sea
chapters.artPrompt: a baby elephant holding a giant crab fast with his long trunk on a moonlit seashore, great waves curling around them, silvery night light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: In the very beginning, when the world was new, the Eldest Magician called every animal to him. The world was young and soft, and the sea was very wide. “Each of you shall have a place to play in,” he said. The elephant, the cow, the fish, and the turtle — every one promised to play in its own place and obey.
The elephant’s child holds the giant crab fast with his long new trunk.

But Pau Amma the Crab did not promise. He went up and down the sea, shaking it as he pleased. When he crawled out, the sea followed him and left the land dry. When he plunged in, the sea rushed after and flooded the shore. Twice a day the shore was bare, and twice a day it was drowned. The moon rose, and the Man’s little girl-child was nearly washed away.
New word: tide — the sea rising up the shore and sinking down again, twice a day.

“Who has been playing with the sea?” asked the Eldest Magician, and all the animals said no, for they had kept their promises. Then it was found that Pau Amma had done it. The beach was long and white, and the crab was heavy. The Elephant’s Child went down to the beach and caught him with his new trunk, and held him fast.

“Play in your own place,” said the Eldest Magician. And Pau Amma grew small — small as a stone on the sand, with a hard shell. So he could never again make the whole sea rise and fall, for he was only a little crab.

But the tide did not stop altogether. To this day Pau Amma must come out of his hole twice a day. And the sea follows him a little way up the shore. And twice a day he must go back, and the sea follows him home. The boats go out with the ebb, and come home with the flow. That is why the tide comes in and goes out, for ever and ever.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Cat That Walked by Himself
chapters.artPrompt: a wild striped cat sitting at the mouth of a firelit cave talking to a woman, a dog and a horse resting behind, warm orange firelight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago, when animals were still wild, the Man and the Woman made a warm cave with a fire. The wild Dog came in from the wet woods and made a bargain with the Man. He would help him hunt in exchange for bones. Then the Horse came and carried the Man for hay, and the Cow gave milk for good grass.
The wild cat sits at the mouth of the cave and talks with the Woman.

But the Cat walked by himself, and all places were alike to him. He watched the cave from the wild woods, and he thought the fire looked very warm. So he went to the Woman with a plan. “I will catch mice in your cave,” said the Cat. “Then give me a place by the fire and a saucer of milk.”
New word: bargain — a fair deal: you give me this, and I give you that.

The Woman agreed, and the Cat played with the Baby till it stopped crying and laughed. She was so pleased that she gave the Cat milk and a warm place by the fire. Then the Cat caught the mice, and the Woman praised him again. The cave was quiet, and the food was safe.

But the Cat kept his bargain in his own way. “I am the Cat who walks by himself,” he said, “and all places are alike to me.” He sat by the fire and drank his milk — and yet he was never quite tame. At night he slipped out to the wild woods and did exactly as he pleased.

So it has been from that day to this. The Dog is tame, the Horse is tame, and the Cow is tame. But the Cat walks by himself. He purrs when he is pleased, catches mice for his supper, and goes where he likes. For that is the bargain he made, and he has never broken it.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Butterfly That Stamped
chapters.artPrompt: a wise bearded king in a golden turban sitting on a throne in a palace garden while a little butterfly flutters up to his shoulder, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long, long ago, in the palace gardens of King Solomon, a little Butterfly flew up to the King. The garden was full of roses, and the morning was golden. The Butterfly’s wings trembled, and his voice was small. He was in a great fuss. “O King,” he said, “my wife will not behave. She quarrels and scolds all day. Please stamp your foot, and teach all the naughty wives a lesson!”
King Solomon sits on his throne in the garden, and the little butterfly tells him everything.

Now King Solomon had many, many queens — hundreds of them — and they quarrelled a little too, just as queens do. The King looked at the Butterfly, and he looked at his queens, and he smiled. But the Butterfly fluttered on and on, so at last the King did as he was asked.
New word: stamp — to put your foot down hard and loud.

King Solomon lifted his great foot and stamped — once! The whole world shook, from the palace to the farthest sea. The queens held on to each other. The butterflies held on to their flowers. The golden cups rattled, and the peacocks screamed. Everything was very still after the stamping. Even the sea stood still for a moment, and everyone wondered what would happen next.

The Butterfly’s wife saw that her husband had a friend as mighty as King Solomon. She flew gently back to him, and she was kind and good ever after. And the wife never scolded again, for she had learned her lesson. And the queens now knew what the King’s foot could do. They were gentle and merry with each other from that day on.

Only Queen Balkis, the wisest of them all, smiled, for she had seen the little butterfly fly by. “What was all that?” the queens asked, but the King only smiled again. The butterfly and his wife lived happily in the garden, and King Solomon was at peace at last.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Tabu Tale
chapters.artPrompt: a cave-girl standing tall and polite before the grown-ups of her tribe inside a firelit cave, her hands folded behind her back, warm evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: By and by Taffy grew taller, almost as tall as her mother. She could catch fish, and scratch pictures, and say clever things. But Taffy had one bad habit. She loved to say rude words, and the rudest of them all began with the letter W. And she said them as often as she could.
The grown-ups of the tribe lay a tabu on Taffy, and she promises to keep it.

The grown-ups of the tribe held a talk about Taffy. “She is a big girl now,” they said. “She must learn to be most respectful.” The tribe had rules, and the tabu was the strongest. So they laid a tabu on her — the strongest must-not of all. From sunrise to sunset, Taffy must not say one single W word, nor say anything rude to anybody.
New word: tabu — a very old word for a strict must-not: a thing you simply may not do.

All day long the tabu held. Taffy dropped a fish on her toe — and held her breath instead of shouting. The neighbours’ children said rude words to tease her, and she only smiled. Every time a W word came to her lips, she shut her mouth tight and swallowed it. Her face grew red, but her mouth stayed shut.

When the sun went down, the tribe came together again. Taffy had kept the tabu from sunrise to sunset, and not one rude word had slipped out. The grown-ups were proud of her, and her mother gave her a big hug. The fire was bright, and there was fish for supper. “You are most respectful now,” they said, and Taffy stood as tall as her mother.

From that day Taffy said her W words only in her own head. Out loud she was as polite as she was clever. She went on fishing with her father and drawing pictures on bark. And in time, she helped to teach the whole tribe to write. But that, as Taffy would say, is another story.
